 South America's Rivers Are Overflowing, and Uruguay's Worst Flooding Season Hasn't Begun
 Rising rivers have displaced residents in Salto and Paysandú, while forecasters warn that the region's heaviest rainfall may still be ahead.
 Miguel Paiva 
/
 Published Nov 02 2026, 9:24 AM EST Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on WhatsApp 
 A woman walks along the beach as rain falls off the coast of Montevideo during a storm on November 1, 2026. Though it is difficult to formally attribute a specific event to El Nino, its effects are being felt globally as the weather phenomenon warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns. 
 Photo by Mariana SUAREZ / AFP via Getty Images 
 The Briefing: 
 Uruguay's coastline and northwestern departments are absorbing sustained punishment from storm systems amplified by one of the most powerful El Niño events in the modern climate record.
 The Uruguay River triggered the country's first flood evacuations of the season in Salto on October 10; GDACS confirmed 108 residents displaced in Paysandú Department by mid-October.
 NOAA's October 2026 forecast places an 83% probability on this El Niño surpassing every event on record since 1950 — and Uruguayan authorities are warning that the heaviest rainfall months still lie ahead.
 Violent storms and persistent heavy rainfall have hammered Montevideo's coastline and surrounding departments, delivering a punishing early preview of what Uruguayan officials are warning could be the most intense rainy season in decades — all driven by a Super El Niño that forecasters increasingly believe will rewrite the climate record books. 
 This is not seasonal weather. What is unfolding across South America's Southern Cone is, in the words of the region's own emergency managers, the opening chapter of a climate event with no precedent in modern record-keeping. 
 Rivers Already Over Their Banks 
 Three of South America's most critical waterways — the Paraná, the Uruguay, and the Iguazú — originate in the highlands of southern Brazil and flow southward through the continental interior. All three have been running dangerously high since early October, spilling over into communities across Argentina, Paraguay, and Uruguay well before the peak of the rainy season arrives. 
 In Uruguay, the Uruguay River climbed to nearly 12 meters at Salto on October 10, forcing the city's first flood evacuations of the season and placing the departmental emergency committee on permanent watch. Hydrological records from the Comisión Técnica Mixta de Salto Grande show the dam's average daily discharge jumped from 16,695 to approximately 18,500 cubic meters per second between October 7 and 10 alone — a volume spike that overwhelmed riverside neighborhoods before precautionary evacuations could be completed. 
 By mid-October, the Global Disaster Alert system classified the situation in Paysandú Department as an active flood emergency, with 108 residents displaced and local media confirming additional evacuations still underway as river levels kept rising. 
 Montevideo's Coastline Takes the Brunt 
 For residents along Montevideo's stretch of the Río de la Plata, the convergence of Atlantic storm fronts and surging interior rivers has translated into relentless coastal punishment. Storm surges driven by sustained winds compound an already waterlogged landscape, battering seafront infrastructure and inundating the low-lying rambla neighborhoods that line the capital's shore.

 Montevideo has confronted destructive rainfall events before — a January 2022 storm delivered a month's worth of precipitation within hours, leaving multiple neighborhoods flooded in a single event that city authorities called unprecedented. But the prolonged and compounding nature of this El Niño cycle means conditions do not reset between storms, making a meaningful recovery nearly impossible. Emergency services are being stretched simultaneously across multiple departments, forcing authorities to triage crisis response rather than focus resources on any single zone. 
 What the Science Says About This El Niño 
 The atmospheric and oceanic data underpinning this crisis has alarmed climate scientists since mid-2026. NOAA's October 2026 forecast places a 100% probability on the current event qualifying as "very strong" during the October-to-December window, while assigning an 83% chance that it will reach the rarer "historic" threshold — defined as surpassing every El Niño on record since 1950. That 83% probability, updated on October 8, represents a meaningful increase from the 69% that NOAA reported in its August forecast, reflecting how sharply conditions in the tropical Pacific have intensified over just two months. 
 For South America's Southern Cone, the practical consequence is not a series of isolated intense storms but months of persistent, widespread precipitation with minimal recovery windows between events. Climate models generated as far back as May 2026 projected significant above-average rainfall and severe storms across Argentina, Uruguay, southern Brazil, and Paraguay through the peak summer tourism season. Those projections are now materializing ahead of schedule. 
 The Salto Grande Dam Sends Water Downstream 
 The Salto Grande hydroelectric facility — a binational dam shared with Argentina on the Uruguay River — has become a central focus of the flood management response. As upstream flows intensified, operators progressively opened the spillway gates to relieve mounting pressure on the reservoir , directing excess water downstream into communities already managing elevated river levels. The decision follows standard operating protocol during major flood events, though it extends the downstream impact into Salto, Paysandú, and the Argentine border city of Concordia — all located on the same river corridor below the dam. 
 A Regional Emergency With More to Come 
 The crisis is not contained within Uruguay's borders. On October 18, Paraguayan authorities maintained a red alert in Ciudad del Este as the Paraná River surged , triggering the evacuation of more than 1,200 people. In Argentina's Misiones Province, rising river levels forced additional evacuations and the closure of border crossings, while the Yacyretá Dam opened its spillway to regulate water flow through the Paraná corridor. In Corrientes Province, hundreds more residents were displaced as the regional crisis spread across the tri-border zone shared by Paraguay, Argentina, and Brazil. 
 Uruguayan officials have stopped short of declaring this a peak emergency — because they know the worst is still ahead. Government statements and meteorological forecasters alike confirm that the country's already-saturated northwest faces its heaviest rainfall totals in the months to come, as the Southern Hemisphere summer deepens and the El Niño pattern continues to strengthen into early 2027. 
 For those living along Montevideo's coastline and in the river departments of the northwest, that forecast carries a stark implication: the storms battering the coast today are not the main event. They are the warning.
